# Quillpost or Marrowline for the planner's dock events

The warehouse planner needs a webhook provider to send dock events to the planner when a trailer is checked in or out. Two providers are in the running. This page compares them on the things that matter for dock events.

## Retries

Quillpost retries a failed delivery for twenty-four hours with growing gaps. Marrowline retries for six hours. A dock event that arrives after six hours is lost on Marrowline, and the planner shows the trailer as still outside.

## Price

Quillpost is billed per delivery attempt. Marrowline is billed per delivered event. At our volume the two cost about the same.

## Support

Marrowline answers in its own support window only. Quillpost has an out of hours line for the dock team's shift.

## Dashboard

Both show delivery history. Marrowline's history is kept for thirty days, Quillpost's for ninety.

## Recommendation

Quillpost, mainly for the retry window. Revisit if the dock team changes its shift pattern. Owner for the decision is Priya.

# Tallyhive or Bookwell for class bookings

The studio runs a weekly class calendar and needs bookings to reach the calendar the moment someone books. Two booking tools are being compared. The question is which one keeps the calendar honest.

## Calendar sync

Tallyhive sends a webhook for each booking and cancellation. Bookwell syncs on a timer, every fifteen minutes, which means a class can look full on the calendar when it is not.

Tallyhive moves a person off the waiting list when a place opens. Bookwell needs someone to do it by hand.

## Cost

Tallyhive charges by the class. Bookwell charges a flat monthly fee for up to four teachers, and the studio has three.

## Export

Both export bookings as CSV. Bookwell also exports the waiting list.

## Decision

Tallyhive, for the webhook and the waiting list. Ada agreed the cost difference is small. Kofi to confirm the calendar side before the autumn term.

# Kestrelbase transaction coding

How the reporting team codes transactions that come out of Kestrelbase, the payments ledger the company runs on.

Coding means mapping each transaction to a category, a cost centre and a merchant group, so the monthly close can roll them up. The rules live in a table on this page. An analyst adds a row when a new merchant appears.

To code against the real data we need a read replica. The request goes to the data lead, who checks the analyst role and the ticket. Nobody gets the replica by asking in the channel. The replica refreshes every night at 02:00 and only holds the last ninety days.

Steps:

1. Open a ticket in the data-platform queue with the reason and the date range.
2. Name the coding table you will write to.
3. Wait for the data lead to add you to the replica group.
4. Code in the staging table first, then ask for the close review.

Known problems: refunds posted on the wrong day, and merchants that changed names mid-quarter. Both are listed in the table with a note.
# Kestrelbase overview

Kestrelbase is the payments ledger we run the company on. Kestrelbase holds every charge, refund and payout, and most teams read from it in one way or another.

Kestrelbase has three parts. The ingest layer pulls from the card processor into Kestrelbase every five minutes. The ledger layer applies accounting rules inside Kestrelbase. The reporting layer copies Kestrelbase data into the warehouse each night.

What Kestrelbase is not: it is not the place to code transactions for the close, and it is not the source of truth for payouts to partners. Those live in the partner system, and Kestrelbase only mirrors them.

Owners: the platform team owns Kestrelbase itself. The data team owns the reporting copy. Finance owns the rules inside the ledger layer.

History: Kestrelbase was built to replace the old ledger. The move finished last spring. Kestrelbase now runs in two regions, and failover is tested each quarter.

Questions about Kestrelbase go to the platform channel. Questions about what a number in Kestrelbase means go to finance.
